worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}={e}^{-as}\,L{g(t+a)},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L{u(t-6)({t}^{2}-t+3)}.
$$

Therefore, $a=6,$ and we have 

$$
L{u(t-6)\,g(t)}={e}^{-6s}\,L{g(t+6)},
$$

where $g(t)={t}^{2}-t+3.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+6) & =(t+6)^{2}-(t+6)+3 \\  & ={t}^{2}+12t+36\,-\,t-6\,+\,3 \\  & ={t}^{2}+11t+33.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L{1}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+6)} & =L{{t}^{2}+11t+33} \\  & =L{{t}^{2}}+11L{t}+33L{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+11\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+33\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{11}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{33}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-6)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-6s}\,L{g(t+6)} \\  & ={e}^{-6s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{11}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{33}{s}).\end{aligned}
$$
